Committee: Economic and Financial Affairs Council
Country: People’s Republic of China
Topic: European Energy Crisis
Delegate Name: Hudson Mitchell-Pullman
School: Patrick Henry High School
People’s Republic of China on the European Energy Crisis
The European Union found itself in a precarious situation following the start of the
ongoing war between the Russian Federation and Ukraine. In June 2021, Russia exported just
over 3 billion cubic meters of gas to Europe. These imports accounted for 45 percent of all
European gas consumption, demonstrating the continent’s heavy reliance on Russian energy.
However, after the Ukrainian attacks on the Nord Stream Pipeline in 2022, Russia retaliated by
significantly reducing energy exports. Additionally, many EU countries attempted to punish
Russia by halting all Russian energy imports. These actions caused financial hardship that
stretched far beyond the European continent, causing Europe to seek additional energy
partnerships and thrusting developing nations into energy poverty.1 These new gas partnerships
relied on the rapid adoption of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG), which currently accounts for 37
percent of all European gas consumption. Furthermore, European policymakers and investors
now find themselves at a crossroads between quickly securing Europe’s energy supply and
executing long-term climate ambitions.2 The urgency of the European energy crisis is
underscored by the fact that European energy costs are, on average, double and triple those of the
US, demonstrating the imperativeness of stabilization and reducing reliance on foreign energy
within Europe. However, the European Green Deal aims to make Europe fully carbon-neutral by
2050, requiring the EU to reduce fossil fuel usage and increase investments in renewable energy
initiatives while maintaining adequate energy reserves to ensure stable energy prices.
Following Russia’s weaponization of its energy exports, the United Nations worked to
support impacted developing nations outside of Europe. In 2022, the UN Global Crisis Response
Group (GCRG) published a report outlining how developed nations and local governments can
support developing countries to avoid a severe energy crisis. The report argued for energy
subsidies through price caps, direct cash deposits, and support for public utility companies in
addition to continued investments into renewable energy and global collaboration. Although
these efforts avoided a catastrophic global energy dilemma, some of these measures pushed
economically challenged nations, especially in the Middle East and Asia, into economic hardship
with astronomical national debt. Further, the UN Sustainable Development Goals include global
objectives focused on promoting universal access to affordable and sustainable energy. Although
these goals don’t specifically target Europe, a 2022 UN-Energy report outlines how the UN has
established an energy compact that’s mobilized $600 billion in funding for improving energy
access and a transition to renewables in emerging nations. The report further emphasizes how
supporting these countries is imperative to slowing worldwide climate change.
In 2022, the People’s Republic of China refrained from imposing detrimental sanctions
on Russia. Instead, China increased its crude oil and gas imports while other nations conversely

-clean-energy-transition/
1Northam, Jackie. “Russia Is Using Energy as a Weapon. Could This Spread to the Rest of the World?” NPR.org, 2
Nov. 2022,
npr.org/2022/11/02/1133667483/russia-is-using-energy-as-a-weapon-could-this-spread-to-the-rest-of-the-world.
lessened their reliance on Russian energy. Between March and July of 2022, the Moscow Times
reported that China imported $35 billion in Russian gas, oil, and coal, a 75 percent increase from
the same period in 2021.3 Additionally, this commitment to an energy partnership between these
two nations is exemplified by new partnerships between Beijing and Moscow that enable the
construction of additional natural gas pipelines between the countries.4 In addition to
strengthening fossil fuel ties with Russia, China invested $890 billion into renewable energy
innovation and manufacturing, especially in electric vehicles, solar PV, and energy storage
sectors. The investment represented a 40% increase when compared with 2022, demonstrating
China’s commitment to continue leading renewable energy manufacturing and development
globally.5 Although establishing direct causation between the European energy crisis and this
uptick in investment is impossible, it is plausible that the European energy crisis emboldened
Chinese officials and investors to continue developing the renewable energy industry to
safeguard against future energy calamities. China’s successful actions following the energy crisis
exemplify its commitment to diversifying its fossil fuel sources while also pioneering the global
clean energy revolution through manufacturing.
China and EU member states are uniquely positioned to negotiate partnerships that
stabilize European energy multilaterally. The International Energy Agency (IEA) reports that
China is the leading producer of renewable energy technologies and contains over 60 percent of
the world’s manufacturing capacity.6 This demonstrates that China must work with the EU to
alleviate external supply chain pressures by immediately increasing the quantity of imported
renewable energy technologies manufactured in China and removing all trade barriers. In
addition, many European nations, especially in Central and Eastern Europe, are struggling with
energy storage, particularly LNG and renewable energy storage. With the recent opening of the
world’s largest LNG storage terminal in China, the UN must establish partnerships between
European nations and China to construct additional LNG terminals along Europe’s coastlines.
Additionally, the EU must emphasize the importance of fostering internal alliances between
European countries, allowing for the transportation of LNG between coastal and landlocked
nations. China recommends the European Investment Bank invest $6 billion in additional
pipelines between EU countries. The Chinese National Energy Administration shall invest a
further $3 billion into constructing six medium-sized LNG terminals strategically placed across
Europe. The expected completion of both projects will be July 1st, 2027. Although these
measures will alleviate short-term strain on the European energy market, the EU and China must
embrace more substantive partnerships. This collaboration should involve knowledge transfers,
European manufacturing that utilizes Chinese technology, AI-enabled energy management, and
innovation with new forms of renewable energy, including hydrogen and biomethane. By
mutually adopting the REPowerEU 2022 Plan through unmatched collaboration, China and
Europe’s economy and energy markets will benefit significantly.
